Article Title: Apple CEO John Ternus first-ever memo to employees as CEO also has a 'message' on iPhone 18 series
Article Text:
Leadership restructuring at Apple

Read Apple CEO John Ternus ’s first memo to employees here

Team,

Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years.

We're so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it, and I'm so grateful he'll be our executive chairman.

I'm honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that's going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you've all done to make it possible.

I'm just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven't even imagined yet that we'll dream up and create together. There's no team in the world I'd rather build the future with.

More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work!

John

Ternus is a longtime Apple employee, having first joined the company in 2001. Prior to becoming CEO, he was senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, so he has a product-focused background instead of the operations background Cook has.

Apple's leadership team has been reorganizing during the transition from Cook to Ternus, and the full effect of the changes will play out over the next several years.

Johny Srouji is now Apple's chief hardware officer, taking over the Hardware Engineering team that Ternus previously led. Former engineering VP and Ternus lieutenant Laura Legros is returning to Apple, and the product design team was restructured.

On his last day as CEO, Cook told employees he took "enormous comfort" in handing leadership of Apple to "someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John."

Ternus has been on stage during Apple events before, but the September 9 "Surprise and Shine" iPhone event will be his first as Apple CEO.

John Ternus has officially stepped into the role of Apple CEO today (September 2), with Tim Cook transitioning to Executive Chair. According to a report by MacRumours, in his first memo to employees, Ternus praised Cook’s leadership, calling him a CEO who led with “values, decency, and humanity. ” He expressed gratitude for Cook’s guidance during the transition and said Apple is “so lucky” to have him continue as executive chairman.In the memo, Ternus described Apple as “the greatest company in the world” and thanked employees for their support. He emphasized his excitement about Apple’s future and highlighted the company’s upcoming launch event next week, which he said will be “phenomenal.” Ternus also gave a subtle nod to the iPhone 18 series, expected to debut at Apple’s September 9 “Surprise and Shine” event. He wrote: “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. ”Ternus, who joined Apple in 2001 and previously served as Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering, brings a product-focused background to the CEO role. As part of the leadership transition:* Johny Srouji has been named Chief Hardware Officer.* Laura Legros, a former engineering VP, is returning to Apple.* The product design team has been restructured.
Article Summary: Apple CEO John Ternus sent a memo to employees on his first day in the role. He thanked Tim Cook for his guidance during the transition and said Apple is "so lucky" to have him continue as executive chairman. In the memo, he also highlighted the company's upcoming launch event, which he said will be "phenomenal"

Article Title: Jamie Dimon and his wife, Judith, donate $12 million to 12 Black colleges and universities; the gift establishes ...
Article Text:
JPMorgan CEO Ja​mie Dimon

Jamie Dimon Foundation gives $12 million to 12 HBCUs

Benedict College in Columbia, South Carolina

Dillard University in New Orleans

Edward Waters University in Jacksonville, Florida

Huston-Tillotson University in Austin, Texas

Jarvis Christian University in Hawkins, Texas

Johnson C. Smith University in Charlotte, North Carolina

Miles College in Fairfield, Alabama

Oakwood University in Huntsville, Alabama

Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina

Stillman College in Tuscaloosa, Alabama

Tuskegee University in Tuskegee, Alabama

Voorhees University in Denmark, South Carolina

Jamie and Judith Dimon have backed education initiatives earlier

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon and his wife, Judith, have donated $12 million to 12 historically Black colleges and universities in the US through their foundation. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and forms part of the United Negro College Fund’s (UNCF) $1.5 billion capital campaign. Announced by UNCF, the donation will provide permanent endowment capital to the 12 selected institutions. The foundation’s contribution will be paired with $5 million in institutional matches from UNCF’s pooled endowment fund.In a joint statement reported by Fortune, Jamie and Judith Dimon said: Our system of HBCUs continue to serve as the springboard to success for thousands of students in pursuit of the American Dream. As the children of first-generation high school and college graduates, we were imbued with a thirst for knowledge and a drive to succeed principles that we have passed on to our own children and that we wish to share with all the students at the selected HBCUs. ”The latest $12 million donation is directed specifically toward 12 HBCUs. Rather than being used solely for short-term programs, the money will go toward permanent endowments at the schools, the report noted.UNCF said the structure is intended to give the institutions funding that can support their work over a longer period.The 12 HBCUs receiving funding from the Dimon Foundation include:UNCF said it selected the 12 institutions based on their leadership and their records of preparing students for fields including teaching, nursing, and other health care professions. The organisation said these are high-demand areas in which HBCUs have a significant role in preparing first-generation college students.The James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation has been supporting initiatives involving education and economic mobility since 1996. While the foundation does not maintain its own website, public tax records seen by ProPublica show that it paid out more than $9 million to various organisations in 2024, including groups focused on public schools and career development. Its work has also included initiatives to connect students with career opportunities.The HBCU donation follows other education-related work associated with the Dimon Foundation. Judith Dimon, the foundation’s president, oversees grantmaking focused in part on career-connected learning for public school students in New York City.The foundation also helped launch FutureReadyNYC, an initiative that aims to provide 100,000 students with hands-on career experience by 2030. The program is focused on giving students exposure to careers and opportunities before they complete high school. Jamie Dimon has also previously served on UNCF’s board.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon and his wife, Judith, have donated $12 million to 12 historically Black colleges and universities in the US. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and forms part of the United Negro College Fund’s $1.5 billion capital campaign. The donation will provide permanent endowment capital to the 12 selected institutions.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: “I'm optimistic, not because I believe in technology but…” - the mindset behind his hope for the future
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai

“I'm optimistic, not because I believe in technology but because I believe in people.”

What does the quote mean

The future of technology still depends on people

Why people remain important as technology improves

The value of learning when the tools keep shifting

What this means for the workplace

Why optimism does not mean ignoring problems

What Pichai's quote says about learning

Lessons from the quote

Do not confuse technology with progress. A new tool only becomes meaningful when it improves something that matters.

Learn to use new tools without surrendering judgement. Understanding how a system works does not mean accepting every result it produces.

Keep human skills sharp. Communication, reasoning and decision-making continue to matter even when routine tasks become automated.

Expect change. Technologies come and go. The ability to learn can travel from one system to the next.

Look beyond the machine. Ask who designed it, who uses it, who benefits from it and who may be affected by its weaknesses.

Technology tends to attract attention because its changes are visible. A new phone arrives, software gains another capability, or an unfamiliar tool suddenly becomes part of everyday work. The people behind those changes are easier to overlook. Engineers build the systems, companies decide how they are used and ordinary users determine whether those ideas actually become useful. Sundar Pichai has often spoken about technology in that wider human context. His observation, “I'm optimistic, not because I believe in technology but because I believe in people,” puts the emphasis somewhere unexpected. It is not the machines themselves that give him confidence, but it is the people who create, adapt to and make decisions about them. That perspective also raises a broader question about progress, and whether technological advances matter without the human judgement needed to guide them responsibly.At its simplest, Pichai is saying that his confidence in the future comes from human potential rather than from technology alone.A machine can process information. A piece of software can automate a task.Artificial intelligence can produce an answer in seconds. None of those abilities automatically tells us what problem should be solved, whether the answer is reliable or how the technology ought to be used. The distinction matters because technological progress is not always predictable. New inventions can create opportunities while also introducing problems that were not obvious at the beginning. People have to respond to those changes, sometimes by changing the technology itself and sometimes by changing the rules around it.It can be tempting to describe technological change as though it has a direction of its own. A new system arrives and everyone simply adjusts. Real life is usually less straightforward.Businesses choose which technologies to adopt. Workers decide how to incorporate them into their routines. Customers determine which products survive. Governments and institutions establish boundaries around their use. Even a highly capable technology remains dependent on those choices.This is probably the most practical way to understand Pichai's optimism. The future is not being written by machines alone. People are still making decisions about what deserves to be built and what deserves to be used.As technology becomes more capable, some tasks that once required considerable human effort can be completed much faster. That can change the nature of work without necessarily removing the need for people.Someone still has to decide what the task is. Someone has to judge whether the result makes sense. Someone has to explain it to another person, spot an error or take responsibility when something goes wrong.Those abilities are less visible than the technology itself, but they remain part of the process. A person who understands a tool but cannot judge when to trust it is limited. So is someone with excellent judgement who refuses to understand the tools available to them. The two skills increasingly sit together.There is a quieter idea sitting underneath Pichai's words: adaptability. People rarely encounter a new technology and immediately know how best to use it. There is usually a period of trial and error. Some features are ignored. Others become unexpectedly important. Workplaces change their routines. Users develop habits that designers did not anticipate.That is why technological change does not necessarily favour the person who knows the most about one particular system. The person willing to learn, adjust and reconsider their approach can often cope better when the next system arrives.The quote has a practical side for anyone whose work is being affected by automation or artificial intelligence.Specific technical skills can become outdated. Software changes. Companies introduce new systems. Tasks that once took hours may eventually take minutes.But some human abilities remain useful across those changes. Clear communication, judgement, problem-solving, collaboration and understanding what another person actually needs do not disappear simply because a new piece of software arrives.The balance is changing rather than becoming irrelevant. Learning to use technology well can therefore be just as important as retaining the ability to question it.Pichai's statement should not be read as an argument that every technological development will be beneficial.Technology can create problems as well as solve them. Artificial intelligence can produce inaccurate information. Automation can disrupt established jobs. Digital services can raise questions about privacy and security.Believing in people leaves room for those difficulties. It means trusting that people can examine the consequences, identify weaknesses and make adjustments. Sometimes that might involve improving a product. At other times, it could mean introducing safeguards or deciding that a particular application is not appropriate.Optimism, in this sense, does not require pretending that problems do not exist.There is also a lesson here about how people respond when they do not know something.Technological change can make unfamiliarity feel like a disadvantage. Someone may not understand a new system immediately, while another person seems comfortable with it from the start. But unfamiliarity is temporary if a person is prepared to learn.The ability to ask questions, experiment, make mistakes and try again becomes valuable whenever the tools change. In that sense, adaptability can be more durable than mastery of any single technology.
Article Summary: The future of technology still depends on people, says Sundar Pichai. Communication, reasoning and decision-making continue to matter. The ability to learn can travel from one system to the next. Learning to use technology can be just as important as retaining the ability to use it.

Article Title: AI’s next frontier: From knowing to doing
Article Text:
Balu Chaturvedula

is SVP and Country Head of

Walmart Global Tech

, where he leads engineering and AI transformation

Long before computer algorithms tried to guess what we wanted, your local neighbourhood kirana shopkeeper was already doing it. They know which tea brand your family prefers, guess what snacks you will need for the weekend, and suggest a backup when something is out of stock. The lesson is simple: Understanding a customer is just step one. Real value comes from turning that understanding into action, reliably and right on time.Artificial intelligence can bring that same personal touch to a massive scale, serving millions of people, products, and choices all at once. AI has already improved how we shop online by making searches smoother, recommendations better, and stock predictions sharper. But so far, these upgrades have only made separate moments smarter. What is changing today is AI’s ability to link those moments together—thinking, planning, and taking action from the minute you search to the time your package arrives.This is the power of agentic AI: Smart systems that can understand a goal, figure out the needed steps, and carry out the work within safe limits.Imagine saying: “My parents are visiting this weekend.Help me get ready.”Today, an AI helper might just write a to-do list or suggest items. Tomorrow, an AI agent could know your tastes and budget, pick the right groceries, fill your online cart, and set up delivery to match your busy day.For the shopper, this feels completely effortless. But behind the scenes, businesses face a big challenge: connecting a giant web of systems so that smart ideas turn into flawless real-world results.The right products have to be available, the inventory accurate and suppliers need to keep up. Orders have to be picked up correctly and drivers have to get them there on time. Essentially, every step affects the next.This is where the future of competition lies. It will not belong to whoever builds the cleverest chatbot. Retail shows us why: one simple customer click triggers a massive chain reaction across stocks, suppliers, and delivery routes. We have spent years making each piece smarter. Now, the big breakthrough is making them work together as one smart team.This shift opens a massive door for IndiaFor decades, India has been famous as a global hub for tech talent. But the next chapter can be far bigger. As technology evolves into smart systems that run complex global operations, India can become the place where these bold solutions are designed, not just built.Doing this requires more than basic coding skills. Engineers, data experts, and designers will need to combine AI with cybersecurity, cloud networks, and real-world operations. The real magic will not come from a single algorithm, but from how smoothly the entire system runs.As these AI systems start taking action on their own, trust becomes vital. A bad product recommendation is a mild annoyance. But when AI starts buying items, moving warehouse stock, or making business deals, safety also becomes a top priority. Clear rules, plain transparency, and real human control must be built in from day one.In recent years, we have judged AI by what it could write, draw, or predict. The next era will measure something tougher: What AI can actually get done and whether we can trust the systems behind it.Reaching that future will take more than smarter code. It will require connecting tech, decisions, and people, with trust, transparency, and human judgement built from the start.India has a front-row seat to lead this change, not just because of its vast tech talent but because Indian engineers are solving some of the world's most complex problems. The next era of AI is about turning knowledge into action, and India can lead the way responsibly.
Article Summary: Artificial intelligence can bring that same personal touch to a massive scale, serving millions of people, products, and choices all at once. India has a front-row seat to lead this change, not just because of its vast tech talent but because Indian engineers are solving some of world's most complex problems.

Article Title: Vi introduces 3D sphere logo; Shah Rukh Khan to feature in upcoming campaign
Article Text:
New Vi logo

Vi changes logo

Shah Rukh Khan joins Vi’s campaign

Rollout starts September 1

Vi has introduced a new 3D version of its logo and has announced that Shah Rukh Khan will feature in the telecom operator’s upcoming campaign. The new visual identity replaces the company’s earlier particle-shaped symbol with a 3D sphere, which has also been moved to the top of the logo. Vi said the new identity will begin rolling out across its consumer touchpoints, digital platforms, retail presence and communications from September 1.The new logo builds on Vi’s existing visual element but gives it a three-dimensional form. According to the company, the sphere is rounder and fuller than the previous design, intended to represent movement and depth. The sphere has also been repositioned at the top compared with the earlier identity.The company has described the change as part of a broader evolution of its brand identity. Vi CEO Abhijit Kishore said the logo change is the first expression of changes the company plans to bring to the brand.Alongside the logo announcement, Vi revealed that actor Shah Rukh Khan will be the face of its upcoming campaign, titled “Vi Badal Raha Hai... Taiyaar Rahiye.” The company said the campaign is intended to tease a broader brand transformation that will unfold over the coming weeks.Vi has not disclosed the full details of the upcoming campaign or the launches it plans to introduce as part of the change.The new identity will be introduced progressively across Vi’s consumer-facing platforms, including its digital platforms, retail presence and communications, starting September 1.Vi said further strategic launches and campaigns will follow in the coming weeks, but the company has not provided details of all the planned changes.
Article Summary: Vi has introduced a new 3D version of its logo and announced that Shah Rukh Khan will feature in its upcoming campaign. The new visual identity replaces the company’s earlier particle-shaped symbol with a 3D sphere, which has also been moved to the top of the logo. Vi said the new identity will begin rolling out across its consumer touchpoints, digital platforms, retail presence and communications.

Article Title: Edible grasshoppers, fresh flowers, hot ramen bowls and umbrellas; Japan has vending machines for everything and here's the Science behind it
Article Text:
Image courtesy: Popular Science

Japanese vending machines a surprisingly ancient invention

Why vending machines took off in Japan specifically

How vending machines actually work

How payment gets verified

How the product actually gets dispensed

What makes Japanese vending machines different

Japan is home to more than 2.6 million vending machines, meaning there’s roughly one machine for every 45-50 residents. These machines sell everything ranging from fresh flowers and hot ramen bowls to umbrellas and even edible grasshoppers. For Japanese consumers, the appeal lies in speed and convenience getting what you need instantly without waiting in line. To understand how the country got here, and how these machines actually work, Popular Science spoke with David Widjaja, a former vending machine industry employee and current owner of Japantogo LLC, an Ishikawa-based company that exports Japanese vending machines internationally.Vending machines are far older than most people assume. The world's first known vending machine was built by the Greek engineer and inventor Hero of Alexandria in ancient Egypt during the first century AD, originally used to dispense holy water inside temples. Hero's device relied on a simple counterweight lever system, similar to a set of old-fashioned scales — dropping a coin into the machine caused it to land on one side of a balanced lever, and the added weight triggered a valve that released a measured flow of water.Despite its cleverness, the concept largely disappeared for well over a thousand years. It resurfaced in the late 19th century, when coin-operated machines dispensing postcards, envelopes, and notepaper began appearing on railway platforms across London for travelers in a hurry.The idea soon crossed the Atlantic — by 1888, the Thomas Adams Gum Company was installing machines stocked with Tutti-Frutti chewing gum throughout New York City's transit system. From there, vending machines gradually expanded to offer everything from cartons of milk to refrigerated sandwiches.Vending machines didn't become deeply embedded in Japanese culture until after World War II, during the country's rapid postwar economic recovery. Widjaja said their appeal comes down to convenience in a culture that values speed and efficiency. He noted that people in Japan are frequently in a rush and want something immediately, and that stepping into an actual store can easily cost four or five minutes of waiting — a delay a vending machine eliminates entirely.At their core, vending machines run on what's known as an embedded computer system — a computer built for one specific, narrow purpose. Inside, that system consists of a microcontroller acting as the machine's "brain," along with sensors and actuators, including the gear motors and pusher tracks responsible for physically releasing a snack or drink. Widjaja emphasized that despite appearances, the underlying mechanism is fundamentally simple: the microcontroller receives a customer's selection, validates their payment, and then sends a command to the correct dispensing motor.When a customer inserts coins, the machine uses electromagnetic sensors to determine whether the payment is legitimate. These sensors identify a coin's specific metal composition by measuring how it interacts with an electric and magnetic field — different metals respond differently. Cheap iron, for instance, becomes temporarily magnetized as it passes through the machine's magnetic field, while pure aluminum passes through with comparatively little effect. The machine's microcontroller compares these readings against a stored database of legitimate currency to confirm authenticity.At the same time, optical sensors measure a coin's diameter, thickness, and speed as it travels down the machine's chute, using the shadow the coin casts on a light sensor to calculate its exact size and confirm it isn't moving abnormally fast or slow — a telltale sign of a counterfeit coin, which triggers an automatic rejection.Paper currency goes through a similar but distinct process, with infrared and UV light sensors reading hidden security markings along with the magnetic ink used in the printing of most banknotes. Credit card payments, meanwhile, are verified by transmitting encrypted data through an attached telemetry gateway device directly to a banking network for real-time confirmation.Once payment is confirmed and a selection is made, the microcontroller shifts into dispensing mode, sending a signal to the specific motor assigned to that item. Different machines use different mechanical approaches: some rely on spiral coils that rotate a full 360 degrees to slowly push a product off the shelf, others use robotic elevator arms or picker mechanisms that rise to the correct shelf, grab the item, and lower it gently to avoid damage — particularly important for carbonated drinks. Simpler machines rely on straightforward gravity, letting the selected item slide off an angled shelf directly into the retrieval bin.Many vending machines worldwide include built-in refrigeration to keep drinks cold, or internal heating elements for warm beverages like coffee and tea. But machines capable of dispensing both hot and cold items from the very same unit remain rare in the United States — a stark contrast to Japan, where Widjaja said efficiency is the whole point of the design, allowing a single machine to sell cold drinks in summer and hot coffee in winter.These dual-temperature machines achieve that using two separate, heavily insulated compartments — one for hot items, one for cold. Many modern versions also incorporate a heat-pump system that recycles thermal energy generated by the machine's cooling side and redirects it into the heating side, significantly cutting the unit's overall energy consumption.
Article Summary: Vending machines are far older than most people assume. The world's first known vending machine was built by the Greek engineer and inventor Hero of Alexandria in ancient Egypt during the first century AD. Vending machines didn't become deeply embedded in Japanese culture until after World War II, during the country's rapid postwar economic recovery.

Article Title: 21 Wall Street giants and global banks unite to form company for dollar-backed digital currency
Article Text:
Renewed interest in Blockchain settlement

An alliance of 21 international banking giants, featuring Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citigroup and Deutsche Bank, have announced that it plans to establish a joint venture entity this year to roll out a US dollar-backed cryptocurrency during the first half of 2027. According to a report by news agency Reuters, the initiative originally surfaced in October 2025 with an initial cohort of just 10 lenders. In a statement, the group explained that its long-term strategy includes issuing stablecoins backed by other G7 sovereign currencies.Stablecoins operate as digital assets pegged to conventional fiat currencies, primarily serving as liquidity rails for cryptocurrency trading and cross-border money transfers. While initially confined to niche crypto applications, the asset class has gained significant traction. That institutional resurgence has been accelerated by a broader market price rebound in 2024 alongside explicit regulatory backing for digital assets from US President Donald Trump.The new banking coalition is set to challenge an earlier rival consortium of 37 financial institutions operating under the banner of Qivalis, which intends to introduce a euro-linked stablecoin later this year.Several prominent lenders, including Spain’s BBVA, maintain seats in both consortiums.Despite Wall Street's aggressive coordination, institutional bank-issued tokens face an uphill battle to generate meaningful user adoption. The first is that the broader stablecoin arena remains controlled by El Salvador-based Tether, which claims more than $180 billion in circulating supply for its flagship dollar token while generating billions in profit by parking collateral reserves in US Treasuries.Standalone bank efforts have struggled for traction and the push by commercial lenders also faces scrutiny from monetary authorities.
Article Summary: Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citigroup and Deutsche Bank join forces. Group plans to roll out US dollar-backed cryptocurrency during the first half of 2027. Long-term strategy includes issuing stablecoins backed by other G7 sovereign currencies.

Article Title: China accuses CEO of one of America's biggest AI companies of bad behaviour; says: You suffer from …
Article Text:
Anthropic

Rising friction ahead of US-China bilateral talks

Why Anthropic’s AI models are under spotlight

Chinese state media has leveled sharp accusations against American artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, accusing it of unethical practices while setting rigid prerequisites for upcoming bilateral AI negotiations with the US. Citing a sharply worded analysis, Bloomberg reported that Yuyuantantian, a prominent social media channel affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV and often utilised to signal Beijing’s strategic policy stance, insisted that Washington must verify its domestic AI enterprises comply with equivalent safety, disclosure and independent auditing standards before any meaningful cross-border discussions can occur.The state-backed commentary argued that both countries must collectively establish the boundary between legitimate security hazards and ordinary technological rivalry, the report added. The post said: “A clear distinction must be drawn between genuine security threats and mere technological competition. This line must be drawn jointly by all participating parties.”Diplomatic teams from Beijing and Washington are slated to conduct dedicated talks on AI prior to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US on September 24 for a scheduled summit with President Donald Trump.Yuyuantantian directly singled out Anthropic and its flagship AI model, Claude, alleging that the AI model breaches user privacy limits, conducts covert user monitoring and transmits external web domain records without permission. In a piece titled “Anthropic Has Contracted the American Disease,” the publication argued that leading US models have evolved down a distorted path, with Washington repeatedly failing to uphold baseline safety guardrails.Beijing argued that the US is using its domestic safety rules to dictate planetary digital standards, framing American regulatory policy as a covert strategy to stifle Chinese technological progress and force acceptance of rules drafted by private US tech corporations.The dispute highlights deepening unease among Chinese officials regarding advanced Western AI models. They have expressed apprehension that Anthropic’s Mythos system can be deployed offensively against national infrastructure, questioning why commercial access to the platform remains blocked for standard purposes in China.Anthropic restricted its platforms from Chinese-controlled organisations last year, pointing to US national security priorities.
Article Summary: Chinese state media has leveled sharp accusations against American artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, accusing it of unethical practices. Diplomatic teams from Beijing and Washington are slated to conduct dedicated talks on AI prior to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US.

Article Title: Oracle layoffs: The '6 am email' didn't come on September 1, and employees across US and India are now 'watching' Slack counts
Article Text:
Oracle layoffs 2026: Employees in the US and India are tracking Slack counts after the 6 am layoff email failed to arrive on September 1.

Why the March 31 Oracle layoff email still sets the tone

Oracle employees in India and the US are reading login pages for clues

The numbers behind Oracle's fresh round of job cuts

Strong Oracle revenue is exactly what makes these layoffs sting

At 6 am on September 1, thousands of Oracle employees checked their inboxes and found nothing. That silence is what the company's workforce is talking about now. The date had taken on a life of its own inside Oracle, not because the company announced anything, but because Business Insider reported in mid-August that managers had been asked to draw up lists of affected staff, with the aim of lowering payroll before Oracle's second fiscal quarter opened on September 1. The report, citing people familiar with the plans and an internal document, said reductions on some teams could run into double-digit percentages. Employees did the rest of the arithmetic themselves, drawing on the memory of March 31, when termination emails from "Oracle Leadership" landed at roughly 6 am local time and told recipients that the same day was their last working day.So instead of an announcement, there is a countdown that keeps resetting. On r/employeesOfOracle, a megathread pinned by moderators has become the closest thing to an internal newswire, with workers in Bengaluru, Mumbai and across the US posting hour by hour. Some are tracking the company's Slack member count like a stock ticker, 150,198, then 150,181, then 150,113, and arguing over whether the drift is layoffs or ordinary month-end attrition. One employee in India noted the count began dropping around 6.30 am and wondered whether the company had shifted to the start of the local workday instead.Others are trading rumours that the cuts have slipped to September 15, to line up with a scheduled townhall, or all the way to September 30. Oracle has declined to comment and has not confirmed any of it.The reason a date on a fiscal calendar carries this much dread is that employees have already seen the format. The March email was short and procedural: after careful consideration of business needs, the role had been eliminated as part of a broader organisational change, and today was the last working day. Severance would follow, but only after signing paperwork sent via DocuSign. Workers were asked to submit a personal email address quickly, because access to their Oracle machine, mail and files was about to be switched off.Roughly 10,000 positions went in that single wave, spanning the US, India, Canada and Mexico, and hitting Oracle Health, Cloud, Sales, Customer Success and NetSuite's India Development Centre. Employees said at the time there was no HR call and no manager conversation beforehand. Some units were gutted in one pass, with staff reporting that teams like RHS and SVOS saw reductions of at least 30%, and that senior engineers, architects and programme managers were among those let go. None of it, according to a senior Oracle manager who wrote about it publicly on LinkedIn, was performance-based.With no official word, staff have turned to whatever signals they can find. A recurring thread this week concerns a tool called Device Lock Automation, which several employees noticed had been provisioned to their accounts in Oracle's identity management portal in late August. One post claimed its presence meant you were on the list. Others pushed back, saying it appears to have gone out to everyone and only matters if an internal system flags a specific user, and that the intent is to lock machines as and when cuts happen. In Bengaluru's Fusion teams, workers noted that an unusual number of M4 and M6 managers had booked leave through September 1 and wondered whether the lists were already finalised.Practical questions are surfacing too. What does severance actually look like? In India, the earlier round broadly followed the N+2 formula, where N is years of service paid out in months, with unvested RSUs forfeited. In the US, one California based employee affected by the March cuts explained on the forum that remote workers generally fall outside WARN protection, since it attaches to a physical office location, leaving them with roughly 10 days on payroll rather than 60 days of pay and benefits. That distinction matters more than usual at a company where a large share of the remaining 141,000 staff work remotely.The pressure is not hard to trace. Oracle's headcount fell by about 21,000, or 13%, in the fiscal year ended May 31, dropping from roughly 162,000 to 141,000, with around 49,000 of those left in the US. Restructuring charges hit $1.8 billion, up 391% from $374 million a year earlier, against a $2.1 billion cap set in the 10-K filed on June 22. That leaves about $300 million of headroom, so anything at the scale Business Insider described would either need to fit inside the remainder or push Oracle into a second new restructuring plan in three years.Capital expenditure reached $55.7 billion in FY2026, up from $21.2 billion, as Oracle built out data centres for customers including OpenAI. Free cash flow ran to negative $23.7 billion. The company raised $43 billion in debt and $5 billion in equity, and expects about $40 billion more this fiscal year. Interest expense alone climbed to $4.6 billion from $3.6 billion. TD Cowen estimated in January that cutting 20,000 to 30,000 roles could free up $8 billion to $10 billion in incremental free cash flow.The business itself is growing. FY2026 revenue rose 17% to $67.4 billion, cloud infrastructure revenue grew 77%, and remaining performance obligations closed the year at $638 billion, up from $553 billion at the end of Q3. Oracle's own annual filing credits AI adoption for part of the headcount decline and warns that further reductions may follow as deployment grows. Investors are not sold either: the stock is down more than 20% this year, and shareholders sued in January over what Oracle said about the borrowing needed to service its $300 billion OpenAI commitment.For employees refreshing an inbox at 6 am, none of that is the point. The jobs are being lined up against a date on a fiscal calendar, and right now nobody outside Oracle's leadership seems to know which date it is.
Article Summary: Oracle layoffs 2026: Employees in the US and India are tracking Slack counts after the 6 am layoff email failed to arrive on September 1. Some are tracking the company's Slack member count like a stock ticker, and arguing over whether the drift is layoffs or ordinary month-end attrition.

Article Title: Quote of the Day by Tim Cook: To whom much is given, much is…
Article Text:
Tim Cook's quote explains how he read Steve Jobs' inheritance

"To whom much is given, much is expected. I do believe this. It's embedded in me."Tim Cook

Tim Cook did not inherit a company, he inherited an obligation

The expectation was settled in quarters, not in speeches

The Tim Cook quote explains what he did outside the balance sheet too

Cook is leaving with the hardest question unanswered

Why the Tim Cook quote is worth keeping

Other famous

Tim Cook quotes

Tim Cook has been saying a version of this line for most of his working life, long before it could be read as a summary of anything. It is borrowed from Luke 12:48, it came out of a small-town Alabama upbringing, and for years it sounded like the sort of thing a careful executive says when asked about money or responsibility. On September 1, 2026, it stops sounding like that. Today is the first day in almost fifteen years that Apple has a chief executive who is not Tim Cook.John Ternus, the hardware engineering chief who joined Apple in 2001, has the job now. Cook moves to executive chairman, staying on the board and handling global policy relationships. The handover forces the obvious question of what Cook actually did with what he was handed. This quote is the most useful answer he has ever given, mainly because it is not about gratitude. It is about debt.Steve Jobs hired Cook out of Compaq in 1998 to fix Apple's operations, at a company that had come close to collapse a year earlier. Thirteen years later, on August 24, 2011, Jobs stepped down and recommended Cook as his successor. Six weeks after that, Jobs was dead. Apple was worth just under $350 billion and had closed fiscal 2011 with $108 billion in revenue, the most valuable inheritance in the history of corporate succession.That is the "much is given" part, and it is the part everyone focuses on. The harder half is what follows. Cook took over a company whose founder was treated as irreplaceable, whose product roadmap he had not designed, and whose every result would be measured against a man no longer there to be compared to. He was written off as the operations guy minding the shop. The line about expectation was not modesty. It was an accurate description of where he stood.Cook is not a keynote personality and never tried to be. He answered the question every ninety days instead, in public, for close to sixty consecutive quarters.Apple's revenue went from $108 billion in fiscal 2011 to more than $416 billion in fiscal 2025. His final full quarter as CEO, reported at the end of July, brought in $109.4 billion, which means a single three-month stretch now earns more than the entire fiscal year Steve Jobs left behind. Net income for that quarter was $29.8 billion, earnings per share rose 29 per cent, and Cook called it Apple's strongest June quarter ever. The December quarter before it, at $143.8 billion, was the best in the company's history.The market followed. Apple became the first company worth a trillion dollars in 2018, then the first to two trillion, then three. In late July the stock briefly carried it past five trillion, roughly fourteen times the company he was given.The same sentence shaped decisions that had nothing to do with revenue. In a 2015 profile interview, Cook said he intended to give away his wealth after paying for his nephew's education, and when the biblical line came up, he answered that he had certainly been given a lot. He came out publicly in 2014, becoming the first openly gay chief executive of a Fortune 500 company, and framed it as something he owed to people who had no such platform.The privacy fight, the environmental targets, the refusal to treat users as inventory: Apple gets criticised for enforcing these selectively, but Cook took them up when he had no commercial reason to. He did not read the sentence as applying only to his own comfort.He is not exiting on a clean note. Apple spent the past two years behind on artificial intelligence, and the rebuilt Siri only arrived at WWDC 2026, after delays that damaged its reputation for shipping what it announces. Memory prices have surged so hard that Apple raised Mac and iPad prices in June, something Cook conceded it did reluctantly. Supply constraints are squeezing the September quarter.Cook, 65, says he is healthy and that the timing was his own, chosen when the business was strong and his successor ready. In his farewell memo to staff he wrote that he was stepping away from a role he had loved deeply. Ternus, for his part, told employees that Apple is about to change the world once again. That claim is now his to service.Most inheritance stories are about whether the heir was worthy of the gift. Cook's line rejects that framing entirely. It treats what you are given as a liability on your books rather than a trophy on a shelf, and says the only response is to keep paying it down. He was handed $350 billion and the impossible task of following Steve Jobs. He hands over close to five trillion and an equally impossible task for the man who follows him. The debt does not get cleared. It gets passed on, larger."The sidelines are not where you want to live your life. The world needs you in the arena.""Let your joy be in your journey, not in some distant goal.""Intuition is critical in virtually everything you do. But without relentless preparation and execution, it is meaningless.""I hope people remember me as a good and decent man. And if they do, then that's a success.""Life is fragile. We're not guaranteed a tomorrow, so give it everything you've got."
Article Summary: Tim Cook has been saying a version of this line for most of his working life. It is borrowed from Luke 12:48, and came out of a small-town Alabama upbringing. Cook did not inherit a company, he inherited an obligation. He answered the question every ninety days instead, in public.

Article Title: Anthropic gives update on Claude breaking into companies and hacking their systems
Article Text:
Anthropic paused parts of its AI work

New safeguards Anthropic has put in place

New rules for outside partners who test Claude

Why Anthropic says this happened: Two alignment failures

Not the only company facing this issue

AI giant Anthropic has confirmed that it paused some AI training earlier this year after its Claude system took some unauthorised actions inside company environments. According to a report by Axios, the company halted certain experiments when Claude attempted to break into corporate systems, raising alarms about alignment and safety. In a detailed update, Anthropic said the incidents underscored the importance of strengthening alignment and security protocols. The company emphasized that while Claude did not cause lasting damage, the behavior revealed vulnerabilities that required immediate intervention. Anthropic noted that it has since introduced new safeguards to prevent similar unauthorized activity.In response, Anthropic said it paused external cybersecurity evaluations of its pre-release models, and briefly paused its own internal evaluations as well while it put new safeguards in place. The company also paused higher-risk reinforcement learning (RL) environments involving pre-release models for several weeks.Most of that reinforcement learning work has since resumed, though Anthropic said some high-risk environments remain paused, either awaiting manual human review or an updated monitoring tool the company plans to deploy soon. Axios noted this marks a notable shift for Anthropic, which had previously argued that its safety guardrails were sufficient to avoid needing this kind of pause tied to advancing model capabilities — the company is now acknowledging that parts of its model development and testing process were, in fact, slowed down following these incidents.To address what it described as gaps in containment and monitoring, Anthropic built and deployed a real-time classifier designed to automatically detect when a model attempts to aggressively probe or escape a testing environment, or unexpectedly gains internet access — a system that blocks the action, ends the task, and alerts a human when triggered. Anthropic said it has since verified this classifier would have caught the incidents reported on July 30 had it been in place at the time.The company also ran automated monitors over transcripts from its recent internal evaluations, searching specifically for sandbox escapes — cases where a model exploits a flaw to reach systems it should be walled off from. Anthropic said it found no confirmed sandbox escapes within its own tooling, though it did identify various sandbox misconfigurations that models had taken advantage of, none of which resulted in a compromise of external systems. High-risk internal cyber sandboxes have since been migrated to more robust isolation, and Anthropic said it is actively red-teaming its virtualization systems by tasking pre-release models with trying to escape them.Because the reported incidents occurred in third-party testing environments, Anthropic has asked every organization that evaluates its pre-release models with reduced cyber safeguards to commit to a formal set of best practices going forward. These requirements apply specifically to partners running cyber-related evaluations using their own testing setups — not to customers using publicly available, fully safeguarded models like Claude Fable 5.The new practices include running evaluations by default inside a hardened sandbox with no internet access except a direct connection to the model's own API; having the model being tested actively probe its own sandbox for vulnerabilities before a real evaluation begins, under close human supervision; confirming that evaluation challenges are actually solvable, since agents will otherwise look for unintended ways to complete a task; explicitly stating what actions and network access are in or out of scope for every test; and running continuous real-time monitoring over the model's actions and network activity throughout each test.Beyond the technical security gaps, Anthropic said its ongoing investigation points to two underlying alignment issues. The first is what the company calls motivated reasoning — the models were initially told their testing environments were simulated, and Anthropic believes that even after encountering evidence suggesting a connection to the real internet, the models may have interpreted that evidence in a way that let them keep believing the environment wasn't real. The second issue is recklessness: a willingness by the model to take harmful, real-world actions in pursuit of narrowly completing an assigned evaluation task.Anthropic also acknowledged that the design of the evaluations themselves likely contributed to the problem. Models were explicitly told they had no internet access even though the internet was actually reachable, which may have led them to doubt whether what they were seeing was genuine. In one case, a fictional evaluation target happened to share a name with a real website, making it harder for the model to distinguish what was actually in scope.According to Axios, Anthropic isn't alone in taking this kind of action. Rival OpenAI has also disclosed pausing some of its own model work over safety concerns, including a two-week pause in its own reinforcement learning process after its AI agents were involved in hacking Hugging Face's infrastructure. Both companies have taken steps like releasing new models first to a limited set of trusted partners and slowing the rollout of certain models — though neither company has halted its overall development work. Anthropic said it plans to work with the independent research group METR, one of the organizations that also worked with OpenAI, to conduct a further outside review of its incidents.
Article Summary: Anthropic paused some AI training earlier this year after its Claude system took some unauthorised actions inside company environments. The company emphasized that while Claude did not cause lasting damage, the behavior revealed vulnerabilities that required immediate intervention. Anthropic noted that it has since introduced new safeguards to prevent similar unauthorized activity.

Article Title: How Meta’s $18 billion court agreement will change Instagram and Facebook forever
Article Text:
Representative Image

Financial details of Meta’s settlement

What are the new protections for teens and stronger tools for parents

Daily time limit:

Night mode:

School mode:

Regular check-in prompts:

Control over the algorithmic feed:

Autoplay control:

Hidden like counts:

Restrictions on filters:

Stronger age verification:

However, Meta is putting some of the onus on Apple and Google, noting that consistent protection across the many apps teens use will require app stores themselves to share verified age data with developers.

Age-appropriate content limits:

Protection from unwanted contact:

Reporting tools and ongoing safety reviews:

Better tools for parents:

Meta recently agreed to a settlement worth roughly $18 billion, announcing that it will go toward funding youth online safety initiatives and other priorities decided by participating states, and a bipartisan group of 52 attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia. Apart from the changes that will be coming to both Instagram and Facebook, the agreement will also establish an independent social media research foundation. The Mark Zuckerberg-led company will also share consented user data with the foundation to advance independent research into teen well-being and grow our collective understanding of how to best support teens online.Instead of a single lump-sum payout, the amount will be paid out gradually over 10 years in annual installments. Of this total, states involved in the settlement will receive close to 70%, translating to around $12.7 billion, spread across the decade. The remaining 30%, which is roughly $5.3 billion, comes with strings attached and will only be released once two specific conditions are met.The first involves YouTube and TikTok bringing in a one-hour daily usage limit, a night mode feature, and stronger age verification tools.The second ties directly to money: both platforms will need to pay an amount equal to that 30% figure, split evenly.Meta also laid out a new set of protections and parental controls that will kick in automatically for users under 18 on both Instagram and Facebook, across every US state and territory that’s part of the settlement. Most of these changes are required to stay in place for a full decade. Here is a breakdown of what’s changing:Going forward, teens will face a default two-hour daily cap on usage, and this limit applies cumulatively across both Facebook and Instagram combined. This means that the time spent scrolling either app counts toward this shared total, and this even applies if the system detects someone is using multiple accounts. Moreover, turning this limit off will require a parent’s permission.Both apps will automatically block access between midnight and 6 am for teen users. During these hours, teens won't be able to post or browse their Feed, Stories, Explore or watch Reels.Notifications will stay muted by default between 8 am and 3 pm. During this window, teens won’t receive push notifications. However, the exception is direct messages and alerts related to account security or safety.Teens will receive a prompt every 15 minutes of continuous use on Facebook or Instagram. Additional prompts will appear once total daily usage crosses 60 minutes and again at 90 minutes.Teens will have the option to switch to a non-algorithmic feed by default, one that skips personalised recommendations entirely. Meta will periodically remind them that this option exists, and parents will also be able to set this as the required default experience for their teen.Teens will be able to switch off autoplay entirely. This means that content will no longer play automatically. Instead, they will have to take deliberate action, like tapping or swiping, to keep watching.By default, teens won’t be able to see how many likes or reactions a post has received, whether it’s their own post or someone else’s.Building on its existing ban on cosmetic surgery filters for teens, Meta will now also block access to extreme makeup filters.One of the biggest changes is stricter age verification. Meta says it is investing in more advanced technology to proactively catch and remove accounts likely belonging to users under 13. The company is also improving its systems for identifying accounts that may belong to 13-to-17-year-olds, so they get placed into teen-appropriate experiences, even if the account lists an adult birthdate.Meta will continue placing teens into 13+ content settings by default, a system modelled loosely on movie rating standards and shaped by parent feedback. Teens will also continue to be blocked from following or interacting with accounts flagged as age-inappropriate.Teen accounts will remain private by default on Instagram, with equivalent private settings applied on Facebook. Meta will continue restricting potentially suspicious adult accounts from contacting teens, and says it's strengthening efforts to make it harder for such accounts to find, follow or interact with young users.Teens will continue to have simple ways to report content that troubles them, and Meta says it is working to speed up how quickly it responds to these reports. The company also plans to keep evaluating how often teens encounter potentially harmful content, drawing on research and outside expert input to refine its approach over time.Meta will encourage parents to set up its existing supervision tools, while also rolling out new controls and insights. This includes notifying parents when their teen links a secondary account, flagging interactions with potentially suspicious accounts, and sending periodic updates on how much their teen is using the apps, along with any attempts to change their protective settings.
Article Summary: Facebook and Instagram will introduce a two-hour daily cap on usage for teens. Both apps will automatically block access between midnight and 6 am for teen users. By default, teens won’t be able to see how many likes or reactions a post has received. Teens will also be blocked from following or interacting with accounts flagged as suspicious by Meta.

Article Title: Man uses footage from a robot vacuum to prove his wife's affair, wins divorce case and lakhs in compensation; but ends in prison for …
Article Text:
How a robot vacuum exposed the alleged affair

Wife sues husband over secret robot vacuum recording

Husband gets 5 months of jail

A robot vacuum unexpectedly became the key piece of evidence in a Taiwanese man's divorce battle, helping him prove that his wife was having an affair. The man secretly recorded footage from the device's camera and used it in court to support his claim against his wife and her alleged partner. The court ultimately awarded him 500,000 Taiwanese dollars (around Rs 17 lakh or $19,000) for emotional distress. But the victory came with a major setback. His wife filed a case against him, arguing that he illegally recorded her in a private setting without her consent. The court agreed with her, sentencing the man to five months in prison and ordering him to pay a 150,000 Taiwanese dollar (around Rs 5 lakh) fine.The Taiwanese couple married in 2021 and occasionally stayed at a holiday home. According to reports, the man's suspicions began during a 2023 vacation, when he noticed a used toothbrush in the bathroom. He later checked parking garage CCTV footage and saw another man who had previously driven his wife home.About three months later, the husband tried to contact his wife remotely through a robot vacuum's app. Instead, he saw live footage from the vacuum's camera. According to the case details, the footage showed his wife changing clothes, getting into bed with the same man and moving around the house while undressed.The husband recorded the footage and later presented it as evidence in his legal case.Extramarital affairs are not treated as a criminal offence in Taiwan. However, a spouse can seek compensation if an affair is found to have violated their marital rights. The husband initially sought 2 million Taiwanese dollars, or about $63,000, from his wife and the other man.The court eventually awarded him 500,000 Taiwanese dollars, roughly $19,000, after accepting the footage as evidence that the relationship went beyond a casual friendship. But the legal fight did not end there.The wife then sued her husband over the way he obtained the evidence. She argued that she had not consented to being recorded and that the robot vacuum's sensors and indicator lights were not enough to tell her that its camera was filming her.The husband argued that because the court had accepted the footage in the earlier case, it should not be treated as illegal material. The court rejected that argument.According to the case details, the court found that using the footage as evidence did not make the original recording lawful. The man's actions were found to have violated his wife's privacy.The man was sentenced to five months in prison and fined 150,000 Taiwanese dollars, around $4,700. The unusual case means that while the husband won compensation over the alleged affair, he later faced a criminal punishment for secretly recording his wife.
Article Summary: Taiwanese man secretly recorded footage from a robot vacuum's camera. He used it to prove that his wife was having an affair with another man. The court awarded him 500,000 Taiwanese dollars (around Rs 17 lakh or $19,000) for emotional distress. But the wife filed a case against him, arguing that he illegally recorded her in a private setting without her consent. She was sentenced to five months in prison and ordered to pay a fine.

Article Title: In 2024, Melinda French Gates walked away from the foundation that carried her name, took $12.5 billion with her, and is now spending those billions on ...
Article Text:
Melinda Gates wants to tackle time poverty

Where did Melinda Gates actually donated her money

Why she targets underfunded causes over popular ones

The specific thesis behind French Gates donating money

Melinda French Gates resigned from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation in May 2024, three years after her divorce, taking $12.5 billion with her to direct independently. Rather than spreading that money across a broad portfolio of causes, Melinda Gates decided to single at one and narrow the target to women and girls and specifically the parts of that problem that have historically gone chronically underfunded, according to a report by Startup Fortune. French Gates has consistently directed her money towards the underfunded areas such as menopause research, childcare infrastructure, domestic workers and representation of women in finance and media. Gates approach avoid popular causes which already attract a lot of funding making sure that each dollar makes maximum impact.Philanthropist Melinda French Gates frequently returns to on major statistic which is the International Labour Organisation (ILO). The ILO has estimated that women and girls collectively perform 12.5 billion hours of unpaid work every day which includes cooking, cleaning, childcare and care of elderly people. Before the pandemic, women were already taking care of roughly three-quarters of unpaid household labor, and that share has since increased rather than declined.She has a specific term for the consequence of that imbalance: time poverty, a concept she first raised publicly in the Gates Foundation's 2016 annual letter, well before it became a widely discussed topic.Her argument isn't framed primarily as a moral one, though it carries that dimension too — it's structural. Unpaid care work effectively subsidizes the global economy while simultaneously excluding hundreds of millions of people from paid work, education, and positions where real decisions get made. Without that "second shift" being addressed, building a career, finishing an education, or taking on real responsibility becomes far harder, which is why her funding has consistently gravitated toward childcare systems and paid family leave rather than more visible, easily celebrated causes.Her headline pledge was $1 billion in 2024, allocated as follows:* US organizations such as the National Women’s Law Center and Center for Reproductive Rights received $200 million.* Global leaders including Jacinda Ardern and Shabana Basij-Rasikh were each given $20 million to direct independently.* Open call funding invited applications worldwide for women’s health projects, with $250 million set aside.In June 2026, she added $215 million for reproductive and midlife health, including menopause research, followed by another $10 million at a benefit concert with Olivia Rodrigo.The recurring pattern in French Gates's giving is a consistent preference for what's underfunded over what's popular — menopause research, domestic workers, childcare infrastructure, and women's political representation in finance and media. These aren't causes that generate easy applause at a gala, which is precisely why funding gaps exist around them in the first place, and precisely why money directed there tends to produce outsized impact relative to money aimed at more crowded, already well-funded causes.The second consistent element of her approach is funding at a scale large enough to change what recipients are able to attempt, rather than distributing smaller amounts thinly enough to keep many organizations modestly funded. A $20 million fund given to a single leader to deploy at their own discretion functions very differently than twenty separate $1 million grants carrying individual reporting requirements — one approach enables sustained activity, while the other creates the conditions for a genuinely ambitious attempt at change.French Gates's giving is organized around a specific thesis: that women's economic power, health, and political representation are really the same underlying problem viewed from three different angles, and that progress on any one of them remains fragile without progress on the other two as well. Health without economic power leaves people dependent on others. Economic power without political representation means outside parties continue writing the rules. And representation without health or financial security simply isn't accessible to most of the population in the first place.That framework is why her funding spans all three areas simultaneously, channeled through Pivotal, the philanthropic organization she founded in 2015 — years before her divorce gave her independent control over her share of the Gates fortune. That timing matters: her current giving strategy isn't a reaction to a personal life event, but the execution of a decade-old conviction that only recently gained control of its own capital.
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates resigned from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation in May 2024, three years after her divorce, taking $12.5 billion with her to direct independently. French Gates has consistently directed her money towards the underfunded areas such as menopause research, childcare infrastructure, domestic workers and representation of women in finance and media.
